elements.element: The licence extends to Customer's affiliates.
elements.evidence: Inserted clause: "Upon written notice to Commerce One, the licenses granted to Corio under this Section 2 shall extend to Corio's affiliates (any entity that controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with Corio)." No pre-existing affiliate concept existed in the grants, which ran to Corio alone.

elements.element: The licence extends to contractors acting on Customer's behalf.
elements.evidence: Neither Sections 2.1/2.2 nor the inserted clause mentions contractors or subcontractors acting on Corio's behalf; the grants remain limited to Corio (and now its affiliates). To reach preferred, the drafter must add "and contractors acting on Corio's behalf" to the Section 2 grant/extension.
Section 2.2: "royalty-free, fully paid up, perpetual right and license in the Territory".

The express "irrevocable" wording appears only in the fee-bearing Section 2.1 grant; the fully paid-up Section 2.2 grant is "royalty-free, fully paid up, perpetual" with no irrevocability. Preferred requires inserting "and irrevocable" into Section 2.2.

elements.element: A subscription licence is terminable only for uncured material breach.
elements.evidence: Conditional element whose condition does not apply: both Section 2 grants are perpetual (2.1 fee-bearing perpetual/irrevocable; 2.2 fully paid up perpetual); no subscription-term licence is granted, so there is no subscription licence to restrict.

elements.element: The licence is transferable to Customer's successors.
elements.evidence: Sections 2.1 and 2.2 are "nontransferable (except in accordance with Section 14.1)", and Section 14.1 permits assignment "in connection with the merger or acquisition of such party or the sale of all or substantially all of its assets" without consent, and binds successors and permitted assigns. The direct-competitor consent carve-out is a minor limitation, not a material failure.

elements.element: Customer's affiliates are covered on written notice.
elements.evidence: Inserted clause conditions the extension precisely on notice: "Upon written notice to Commerce One, the licenses granted to Corio under this Section 2 shall extend to Corio's affiliates...".

elements.element: The licence is transferable to a successor in a merger or acquisition transaction.
elements.evidence: Retained Section 14.1: "either party shall have the right to assign this Agreement in connection with the merger or acquisition of such party or the sale of all or substantially all of its assets related to this Agreement without such consent", carried into the grants via the "except in accordance with Section 14.1" proviso.

reasons: Fallback level is complete: the single inserted affiliate-extension clause supplies the notice-conditioned affiliate coverage, and the retained Section 14.1 M&A assignment right (incorporated into the Section 2 grants by the "except in accordance with Section 14.1" proviso) supplies successor transferability.

Preferred remains incomplete on two elements: (a) no contractor extension anywhere in Section 2, and (b) the fully paid-up Section 2.2 grant is perpetual but not expressly irrevocable. These are the exact operative repairs needed if the preferred level is pursued.

Minimality holds: one concise insertion addressing only the failing fallback element, with a short parenthetical control definition necessary because "affiliate" is otherwise undefined in the Agreement. Corio is a single defined entity, so there is no duplicate affiliate coverage; Sections 2.1, 2.2, 2.10 and 14.1 are left verbatim, with no survival tails, expense language, or other extras.

Intent is preserved: the extension operates on "the licenses granted to Corio under this Section 2" without disturbing the Territory limit, the Corio Servers installation restriction, the revenue-sharing/expansion mechanic in 2.10, or the Section 14.1 consent regime; no new Vendor assignment exception is created and no cross-reference is left dangling.
Minor point correctly relegated to the rationale rather than redlined: the Section 14.1 direct-competitor consent carve-out narrows, but does not defeat, the M&A successor transfer.
